title: Longitude: The True Story of a Lone Genius Who Solved the Greatest Scientific Problem of His Time
author: Dava Sobel
target_audience: General readers interested in science history
Students and enthusiasts of navigation, astronomy, and invention
Readers interested in biographies of historical innovators
Fans of narrative nonfiction and historical problem-solving
core_themes: The problem of determining longitude at sea
The history and impact of navigation technology
Recognition and reward in the scientific community
primary_purpose: To chronicle the dramatic story of John Harrison, the self-taught English clockmaker who overcame the dismissals and rivalries of the scientific establishment to solve the centuries-old problem of determining longitude at sea, through the invention of an accurate marine chronometer, and to explain how this achievement revolutionized navigation and global exploration.

structure_format.narrative_style: Engaging, narrative nonfiction with a strong storytelling element
structure_format.organization: Arranged chronologically, following the historical timeline from the early quest for longitude to the eventual triumph of John Harrison, interspersed with contextual historical details
features: Descriptions of scientific principles and challenges
Profiles of key figures, including Harrison and his contemporaries
Maps, illustrations, and occasional diagrams (in some editions)

key_concepts_lessons: Longitude was a fundamental problem for centuries, resulting in catastrophic navigational errors and maritime disasters.
Political and monetary incentives, like Britain’s Longitude Act and the huge cash prize, spurred innovation and global competition.
John Harrison’s mechanical genius, perseverance, and attention to detail enabled him to build precise marine clocks that changed navigation forever.
Institutional science can be slow to accept revolutionary solutions, especially from outsiders.
A single determined individual can profoundly influence the course of science and history.
Technological innovation often requires both inventiveness and advocacy to gain recognition.
style_tone: Occasionally poetic in describing the sea and the stakes
notable_features: Blends biography with history of science
Focuses on both personal and societal implications of a scientific breakthrough
Highlights institutional challenges to individual creativity
Short, tightly structured chapters for accessibility
International bestseller and widely used in educational contexts
cultural_historical_context: Set in the 18th century during the Age of Exploration and Enlightenment, the book connects technological challenges with Britain’s naval supremacy and the global push for scientific progress. Published in the late 20th century, it tapped into renewed interest in historical innovations and individual achievements in science.
reception_impact: Became an international bestseller and a staple in science writing
Praised for making a complex scientific and historical puzzle accessible and engaging
Credited with reviving popular interest in John Harrison and chronometry
Adapted into a television film and inspired museum exhibitions
Some critics note a strong focus on narrative at the expense of deeper technical analysis
comparable_titles: The Map That Changed the World by Simon Winchester
The Clockwork Universe by Edward Dolnick
A Short History of Nearly Everything by Bill Bryson (contextual similarities)
